title: Memory Separations from a Collective-Spin Quantum Register
abstract: A spin one-half driven only by total-spin operators generates a renewal process in which one interevent time $n^\ast$ is forbidden while all others occur. No classical hidden Markov model reproduces it with fewer than $1+\sqrt{n^\ast}$ states, an unbounded separation whose only resource is one relative phase of $π$. With $K$ amplitudes the same interference yields $K(K{+}1)/2$ decay channels, and for positive weights and generic rates the classical cost is exactly $K(K{+}1)/2$ states. Both are realized by a depth-three circuit whose parameter count does not grow with the register.
summary: This paper proves a separation between the resources needed by quantum versus classical models to simulate certain stochastic processes. Using a spin-one-half quantum memory, the authors show that enforcing a forbidden event time or generating specific decay patterns requires exponentially more states classically than quantum mechanically. This highlights the computational advantage of quantum memory in describing complex physical dynamics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental separation between the resources required by quantum memory versus classical memory to generate specific stochastic processes.
main_result: It demonstrates that generating a process with a forbidden interevent time requires an unbounded number of states in any classical Hidden Markov Model, while the quantum resource only requires a single relative phase shift.
method: The analysis uses the framework of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and compares the Hankel rank of the process matrix (quantum side) against the required state count (classical side).
model_or_system: The system is a quantum memory implemented in a spin-one-half register driven only by total-spin operators, analogous to an atomic ensemble or spin-squeezed sample.
key_observables: Interevent time distribution $d_n$, the number of required classical HMM states, and the number of decay channels generated by $K$ amplitudes.
important_parameters: The forbidden time $n^*$, the number of amplitudes $K$, and the relative phase $\pi$.
main_assumptions: The classical cost comparison is restricted to finite-dimensional HMMs, and the quantum memory is driven only by collective operations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the structure of the quantum block; Figure 2 shows the classical expense of a forbidden interevent time; Figure 3 visualizes the decay channels generated by $K=3$ amplitudes.
paper_structure: The paper first analyzes the constraint imposed by a forbidden interevent time, establishing a lower bound on classical states. It then examines the decay channels generated by $K$ amplitudes, proving a separation between the quantum cost (related to $K$) and the classical cost ($K(K+1)/2$).
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, physical realization (collective spin register) to demonstrate a resource separation, which is a core theme in quantum information theory, particularly concerning simulation complexity.

FIG. 2. Why a forbidden interevent time is expensive clas- sically, in the edge-emitting convention of Ref. [4], in which each transition carries an emitted symbol and a weight. Every edge shown belongs to the no-event block A, an event ending the interval. Since dn = cTAnb with all factors nonnegative, dn∗= 0 holds exactly when no walk of length n∗joins supp b to supp c, and because the zero pattern of An is periodic from an index at most (D−1)2 +1 onward, retaining walks of every other length forces n∗≤(D−1)2.

FIG. 3. Channels generated by K = 3 amplitudes with base rates (12, 6, 2) and phases (0, 1.1, 2.3). Bars are equally spaced and the tick labels give the true rates. Dark bars at γ = 12, 6, 2 are populations, weights 1.000, 0.640, 0.360. Light bars at the pairwise averages γ = 9, 7, 4 are inter- ference, weights +0.726, −0.800, +0.348. The channel at γ = 7, the average of 12 and 2, has negative weight because cos(ϕ1 −ϕ3) < 0, so it exists only as destructive interference.
